A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites so pages load faster no matter where a visitor happens to be. Without one, every request travels back to a single origin server, the original computer where a website's files live permanently. That trip can be slow if the visitor is far away. To fix this, copies of the content get placed on servers closer to people, called edge locations, since they sit near the "edge" of the network, closest to homes and offices. When someone opens a page and the nearby edge location already has a saved copy ready to serve, that is called a cache hit, meaning the answer arrived quickly without bothering the distant origin server at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries holding copies of a popular book, so readers do not need to travel to one central library across town every time. If an edge location does not have the content saved yet, it fetches it once from the origin server, delivers it, and keeps a copy for next time. This setup reduces waiting time, prevents the origin server from getting overwhelmed, and keeps things running even during traffic spikes or partial outages. It works quietly in the background, but it plays a major role in why websites and videos usually load quickly and reliably today.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | It is the ultimate source everything else copies from |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding saved copies of content | It shortens the distance information must travel |
| Cache hit | A request answered instantly from a saved copy | It speeds up loading and reduces strain elsewhere |
| Content delivery network | The whole network of edge locations working together | It keeps websites fast and reliable worldwide |
